analysis.one_liner: Adds nursing home, in-home care, and outpatient prescription drug coverage to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the 105th Congress; after its January 1997 referral to two House committees and two subcommittees, no further action was ever recorded, and it drew zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made Medicare pay for long-term care—nursing facility care and in-home help—for people who cannot perform everyday activities like bathing, dressing, and eating without help. It would also have added outpatient prescription drug coverage to Medicare for the first time, with a $250 yearly deductible in 1999, government-set payment limits on what pharmacies could charge, required pharmacy participation agreements, and annual reporting on drug price increases. Medicare at the time covered essentially no outpatient prescription drugs and no chronic long-term care, so these costs fell entirely on seniors and their families.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who are 'dependent individuals'—people unable to perform at least two activities of daily living without help, or with comparable cognitive impairment—would gain coverage for nursing facility care and in-home services like aide visits, personal care, and therapy. All Medicare beneficiaries would gain coverage for outpatient prescription drugs after meeting the deductible, with Medicare paying 80% of the cost up to government-set payment limits. Families who currently pay out of pocket for home aides, nursing homes, or prescriptions would see those bills shifted to Medicare.

how_it_helps.text: Extends Medicare Part A to cover extended care services for 'chronically dependent individuals'—those unable to perform at least three activities of daily living—rather than only after a hospital stay.

Adds in-home care—nursing, aide and homemaker services, personal care, therapies, medical supplies, and caregiver training—to Medicare Part B for dependent individuals, delivered through a case management plan.
Creates the first Medicare outpatient prescription drug benefit: coverage begins after a $250 deductible in 1999, with Medicare paying 80% of charges up to a government-determined payment limit.

Requires pharmacies to sign participation agreements barring them from charging Medicare beneficiaries more than the general public, and caps what Medicare pays for multiple-source drugs at the median of average wholesale prices, with a $5 per-prescription dispensing allowance.
Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to publish an annual price guide for physicians covering at least 500 commonly prescribed drugs and to report twice a year on drug price increases.

analysis.who_pays: The long-term care expansion would draw on the Medicare Hospital Insurance (Part A) trust fund, and the drug benefit on the Supplementary Medical Insurance (Part B) trust fund, which is financed by beneficiary premiums and general federal revenue. The bill authorizes appropriations without any dedicated financing or offsetting cuts. Pharmacies would bear new obligations—participation agreements, audits, electronic claims reporting, and payment limits that cap their reimbursement below actual charges in some cases. Drug makers would face price surveys, civil penalties for withholding price data, and public reporting on price increases, though they would also gain a large new paying customer base.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare trust funds, taxpayers, pharmacy margins

drawbacks.text: The bill creates two large new entitlements—chronic long-term care and a universal drug benefit—without any dedicated financing, tax increase, or spending offset, which would have drawn down the Hospital Insurance trust fund and increased Part B premiums for beneficiaries.

The drug benefit includes significant cost-sharing: a $250 deductible that grows each year with Part B premium increases must be met before any coverage begins, and beneficiaries still owe coinsurance afterward, so seniors with modest drug costs would get little or no help.

The bill prohibits the Secretary from using a formulary to exclude specific drugs or classes, and sets payment limits tied to average wholesale prices—mechanisms that critics of the era argued would do little to control rapid drug price growth while adding substantial administrative machinery.

Pharmacies would have to accept government-set payment limits, per-prescription allowances, audits, and electronic reporting, and prescriptions would be capped at 30-day supplies (up to 90 days in limited cases), raising compliance costs and possibly causing some pharmacies to decline participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries, the benefit is substantial: in 1997 Medicare covered neither chronic long-term care nor outpatient prescription drugs, so families bore the full cost of home aides, nursing homes, and medications—often the largest expenses of old age. The bill's weaknesses are fiscal, not conceptual: it imposes the cost on the trust funds without any offset, and its drug benefit is comparatively stingy, with a growing deductible and no formulary or manufacturer price controls beyond reporting requirements. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the long-term care expansion in particular would be very expensive and that the bill's price-control provisions were modest.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees for the entire two-year Congress and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Eliot Engel introduced the Comprehensive Long-Term Care Act of 1997 in the House on January 9, 1997.
No other member cosponsored the bill; it ended the Congress with zero cosponsors.

The bill was referred to both the Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, and within three weeks was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health.
No hearing, committee markup, or floor action is recorded after those subcommittee referrals, and the bill never received a vote in either chamber before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacies and drug manufacturers never had to operate under the bill's payment limits, participation agreements, and price reporting, and private long-term care insurers kept a market free of a Medicare long-term care benefit. Seniors and disabled beneficiaries continued to pay out of pocket for prescription drugs and long-term care, as they would for nearly a decade more—Medicare did not add a drug benefit until 2006.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacies, drug makers, private LTC insurers

for.name: Rep. Eliot Engel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; chaired by Rep. Thomas Bliley (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 9, 1997, referred it to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and took no further recorded action—no hearing or markup—in the two years that followed.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of secondary referral (Medicare financing jurisdiction); chaired by Rep. Bill Archer (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 9, 1997, referred it to its Health Subcommittee on January 21, 1997, and took no further recorded action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was never voted on, so no roll calls exist; a single Democrat sponsored it and not a single member of either party signed on, and the two committees that let it sit were both chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would hand pharmacies a vast new customer base by making Medicare pay for outpatient drugs, but only for pharmacies that sign participation agreements accepting government payment limits, audits, and electronic reporting. Its payment limits and per-prescription allowance would cap dispensing margins below prevailing charges for some drugs.

Universal Medicare drug coverage would expand the market for prescription drugs, but the bill pairs that with government price surveys, civil penalties for withholding price data, payment limits based on average wholesale prices, an annual physician price guide, and twice-yearly reports on manufacturer price increases—tools aimed squarely at drug pricing.

The bill creates a Medicare-funded in-home care benefit—aide services, personal care, therapies—provided by home care agencies, opening a large new revenue stream for the industry that also serves families' need to keep disabled relatives at home.
Extended care for chronically dependent individuals would be paid on a Medicare fee schedule, adding a payer for residents whose care is now financed privately or by Medicaid.

A Medicare long-term care benefit would compete directly with private long-term care insurance policies, which families buy precisely because Medicare does not cover chronic nursing home or in-home care.
